chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdillah, from Bahr al-Saqqa, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Bahr! Good manners are an affluence.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Shall I inform you of a hadith which is not in the hands of anyone from the people of Medina?' I said, 'Yes.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'One day, while the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was sitting in the Masjid, a slave girl of one of the Ansar came to him while he was sitting upright. So she grabbed a side of his clothes. So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) stood up for her, but she did not say anything, and the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did not say anything to her, to the extent that she did that three times.'

So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) stood up for her during the fourth attempt, and she was behind him, so she took an edge of his cloth, then retracted. So the people said to her, 'May Allah deal with you and do (whatever He may)! You withheld the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) three times, neither did you say anything to him nor did he say anything to you. What was your need to him?'

She said, 'For us there is a sick one. So my people sent me to take an edge from his cloth in order to heal him by it. So whenever I wanted to take it, he saw me, and stood up. So I was too embarrassed from him to take it while he sees me, and I disliked to ask him regarding taking it, therefore I took it.'
ai.seo_question: What does the Prophet's patience with the slave girl pulling his garment teach about good manners?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses this narrative to define *husn al-khuluq* not merely as politeness, but as a profound spiritual state of *hayā'* (modesty) and patience that prevents mutual embarrassment. The Prophet’s silence and repeated rising demonstrate that true nobility lies in elevating the other person’s dignity, even when their action is slightly presumptuous. This incident is frequently cited in Shia jurisprudence and ethics to illustrate the virtue of *ihsan* (excellion in conduct) and the importance of considering the social context of one's actions.

en.sarwar: 15. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn abu ‘Abd Allah from his father from Hammad ibn ‘Isa from Hariz ibn ‘Abd Allah from Bahr al-Saqqa who has said the following:

“Abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) said to me, ‘O Bahr, excellent moral behavior is prosperity. Would you like me to teach you a Hadith which is not found in the hands of any of the people of Madina?’ I said, ‘Yes, please do so.’

The Imam said, ‘Once the Messenger of Allah was in the Mosque when a girl from the people of Ansar came in and he was standing there. She held to one end of his (the Messenger of Allah’s) cloth, the Holy Prophet stood up. She did not say anything and he (the Holy Prophet) also did not say anything to her (he then sat down). She repeated it three times

and at the fourth time the Holy Prophet stood up for her and she was behind him. She then took a piece from his cloth and returned back. People rebuked her saying, “May Allah do to you what He may decide to do. You held the Messenger of Allah as your captive. You did it three times. You said nothing to him nor did he say anything to you. What did you want from him?”

She then said, “We had a patient and our people sent me to get a piece from his (the Messenger of Allah’s) cloth to be used to cure the patient. When I wanted to get the piece he saw me and stood up. I then felt shy to take what I wanted when he would see me. I did not like to demand anything from him. At last I took what I wanted to get.’””
